passage: English period note, Rajni. We did riddles today. I asked, "What has hands but can't clap?" Kashish, nine, said, "A clock!" and then added, "And a pair of gloves on a washing line." Later a boy called her "Kashish the Quiz Machine," and she stiffened for a second. Then she saw him grinning, not smirking, and she did a robot voice: "Processing... correct." The class laughed with her. Last term she used to cry at nicknames. Next Friday I will hold a pun hour and talk about teasing that includes versus teasing that hurts.

qa.q: Which riddle did Rajni ask?
qa.a: "What has hands but can't clap?"

qa.q: Why did Kashish decide the nickname was friendly?
qa.a: She felt wary at first and stiffened, but then saw the boy grinning, not smirking, and read it as fun rather than meanness.

qa.q: Why is Rajni's plan to discuss different kinds of teasing useful?
qa.a: It helps children notice cues like a grin or a smirk and learn when teasing is friendly and when it hurts.

qa.q: How might the boy feel when Kashish does the robot voice?
qa.a: Relieved and pleased that she took his nickname as a joke and played along.

grounding: It shows a girl solving riddle logic and reading a nickname as friendly teasing rather than malice.

passage:
Diary, Wednesday.
Gautam Bhaiya looked at my science model and said, "Wow, Deepika, a leaning tower. Very modern." I got angry and said he's mean. Then he laughed and said, "It's a joke! It's nice. Just fix the left leg." I looked again. My volcano stand was leaning a lot. I was still a bit cross, but I laughed too. Later at dinner Papa said, "Oh great, more karela," and Bhaiya winked at me, and I got it straight away: Papa hates karela! I think I understand Bhaiya's jokes better now. Mostly.

qa.q: Which part of the model did Gautam say to fix?
qa.a: The left leg.

qa.q: Why did Deepika get angry at first?
qa.a: Deepika took his "leaning tower" comment as a mean insult before realising it was a joke with a real tip inside.

qa.q: What could Deepika do next time it's unclear whether a comment is a joke?
qa.a: Look at the person's face and ask, "Are you joking?" before getting upset.

qa.q: How might Gautam see his own teasing?
qa.a: He probably meant it as affectionate fun with a helpful hint, not to hurt Deepika.

grounding: It shows a child learning to read an older brother's sarcasm and teasing as playful rather than mean.

passage: At the Tuesday haat in their village, Jagdish Kaka, who sold peanuts, liked to test the children. "Urmila, what goes up but never comes down?" Urmila, ten, frowned at the sky. "A kite? No, that comes down." "Think." She grinned. "Your age, Kaka!" He clapped. Then he said, "Your brain is so sharp, I'll use it to cut my onions." For a moment Urmila wasn't sure. Then she saw his eyes crinkle and laughed. "So I get free peanuts for sharpening?" He poured an extra handful into her paper cone.

qa.q: What did Jagdish Kaka sell?
qa.a: He sold peanuts.

qa.q: Why was Urmila unsure for a moment after the onion comment?
qa.a: She had to decide whether it was a compliment or an odd jab, until his crinkled eyes showed it was friendly.

qa.q: What did Urmila's reply show about handling teasing?
qa.a: Answering with her own joke kept things light and playful instead of taking offence.

qa.q: How might Jagdish Kaka feel when Urmila jokes back?
qa.a: Delighted, which is why he gives her an extra handful of peanuts. 😊

grounding: It shows a girl solving riddle logic and recognising an elder's playful teasing as affection.

passage: In a Toronto school lunchroom, Kwame held up his sandwich. 'Why did the bread go to school?' Esther groaned. 'Because it wanted to be well-bread?' Kwame laughed, 'You always get it!' Later, when Esther spilled her juice, Kwame said, 'Great job, Miss Graceful.' Esther paused, then saw his grin and laughed. 'Thanks, Mr. Helpful,' she said, handing him a napkin. She knew he wasn't being mean; he always teased her when he liked her company.

qa.q: What was Kwame's riddle about?
qa.a: It was about bread going to school.

qa.q: How did Esther feel when Kwame called her 'Miss Graceful'?
qa.a: She paused, unsure at first, then felt amused when she saw his grin, knowing he always teased her when he liked her company.

qa.q: What skill helps Esther handle teasing like this?
qa.a: She checks his face and their history before reacting, which helps her tell playful teasing from real unkindness.

qa.q: What would change if a stranger had called Esther 'Miss Graceful'?
qa.a: She might take it as mean, since she would not have the friendship and cues to read it as playful.

grounding: Illustrates a child understanding puns and light teasing without taking them as malice, set in Canada.

passage: In Class 5, the teacher held a riddle contest. 'What has keys but can't open locks?' Devika's hand shot up. 'A piano!' Omkar muttered, 'Oh, look, our genius.' Devika turned around sharply, then saw him smiling and giving a thumbs up. She grinned and whispered, 'Jealous?' He laughed. Next riddle, Omkar got it right. Devika clapped and said, 'Look who's awake today!' They both burst out laughing, and the teacher shook her head, smiling.

qa.q: What was Devika's answer to the riddle?
qa.a: She said, 'A piano!'

qa.q: What did Devika realise when she saw Omkar's thumbs up?
qa.a: She realised his 'genius' comment was playful teasing, not an insult, so she relaxed and joked back.

qa.q: How could a teacher help students understand teasing like this?
qa.a: She could talk about how tone, smiles and friendship help us tell playful teasing from hurtful comments.

qa.q: How might the teacher see their joking?
qa.a: She seems amused and not worried, seeing it as friendly banter. 🙂

grounding: Shows children understanding riddles and sarcastic teasing as friendly rather than malicious, in a classroom.

passage: I'm Gargi, Pranav's sister. At dinner our uncle said, "Why did the tomato blush? It saw the salad dressing!" Last year Pranav, who's nine, would have asked what was funny. This time he burst out laughing, then said, "Mama, that joke is so old it's a fossil." Everyone laughed. When Uncle pretended to be hurt, Pranav said, "Just kidding," and gave him a high five. I can't be sure what he understands, but he seems to get the jokes now, and to know teasing from meanness.

qa.q: Why did the tomato blush in the joke?
qa.a: It saw the salad dressing.

qa.q: What might Pranav have felt when the family laughed at his fossil comment?
qa.a: He probably felt proud and pleased that his teasing joke landed.

qa.q: How could the family keep building Pranav's humour?
qa.a: Keep sharing puns and riddles and let him try making his own.

qa.q: How does Gargi see Pranav's change?
qa.a: She notices he gets jokes now and knows light teasing from meanness, though she can't be sure.

grounding: Shows a child understanding a pun and using light teasing without malice, seen by his sister.

passage: Monday: Siddharth told his sister Swati, eight, "Nice haircut, did you do it with a spoon?" Swati burst into tears and ran to Amma. Siddharth said, "I was joking!" Thursday: he asked her a riddle: "What has hands but can't clap?" She thought hard, then shouted, "A clock!" and grinned. The next Monday: he said, "Oh great, more homework, my favourite." Swati rolled her eyes. "You're being sarcastic." Then she added, "Nice hair, did you do it with a fork?" He laughed.

qa.q: What was the answer to Siddharth's riddle?
qa.a: A clock.

qa.q: How did Swati feel when she first heard the haircut joke?
qa.a: She felt hurt and upset, taking it as mean.

qa.q: What helped Swati understand the teasing?
qa.a: Playing riddles and hearing sarcasm in low-stakes moments helped her see the playful tone.

qa.q: How might Siddharth feel when Swati teases him back?
qa.a: Amused and relieved that she can now join in the joke.

grounding: Shows a child learning over a week to understand riddles, sarcasm and teasing without seeing malice.

passage: "Disha, I'll tell you about my maths teacher. When I, your Naveen Chacha, was ten, Rao Sir asked the class, 'Why was the six afraid of seven?' Nobody knew. He said, 'Because seven eight nine!' I didn't get it. The boys laughed, and I thought they were laughing at me. I sulked all day. The next morning Rao Sir wrote it on the board: seven ate nine. I suddenly saw it and laughed so loudly the class turned. Rao Sir winked at me. After that, I asked him for a new riddle every week."

qa.q: Why was the six afraid of seven, according to the riddle?
qa.a: Because seven eight nine.

qa.q: What was young Naveen feeling when the boys laughed?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and hurt, thinking they were laughing at him.

qa.q: What turning point in the story helped Naveen get the joke?
qa.a: Rao Sir writing "seven ate nine" on the board the next day.

qa.q: How might Rao Sir have seen Naveen's sulking?
qa.a: He probably noticed Naveen had missed the joke and wanted to help him in on it.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling how as a child he learned to get a pun and stopped misreading laughter as mockery.

passage: The power had gone out in the Bhopal flat, and the fan stopped. Imran, nine, was bored and sweaty. Rehana Aapa lit a candle. "Riddle. What has hands but can't clap?" Imran thought. "A... monkey with no arms?" "A clock!" He groaned. "Another." "Why did the tomato turn red?" "Because it was hot?" "Because it saw the salad dressing!" Imran stared, then burst out laughing. "Dressing! Like putting on clothes!" He laughed so much the candle flickered. "My turn," he said. "Why was the fan sad?" Rehana waited. "Because nobody's a fan of it in a power cut!"

qa.q: What was the answer to "What has hands but can't clap?"
qa.a: A clock.

qa.q: What was Imran feeling when he burst out laughing at the tomato joke?
qa.a: He felt delighted and amused as he suddenly understood the double meaning of "dressing."

qa.q: How could Rehana keep building on Imran's love of wordplay?
qa.a: She could keep swapping riddles and puns with him and help him invent more of his own.

qa.q: How might Rehana feel about Imran's fan joke?
qa.a: She might feel proud and amused that he made his own pun.

grounding: During a power cut, a boy starts understanding puns and makes one of his own.

passage: In the Lucknow kitchen, Rajni burned the toast again. Her older cousin Vandana walked in, sniffed and said, "Wow. The famous chef strikes again." Rajni's face fell. Then she saw Vandana was grinning and already reaching for the butter. "Very funny," Rajni said, trying not to smile. "It's charcoal toast, very healthy." Vandana laughed. "Five stars." Rajni laughed too. She knew Vandana wasn't being mean; she teased like this with everyone she liked. They scraped the black bits off together.

qa.q: What did Vandana call Rajni?
qa.a: "The famous chef."

qa.q: How did Rajni's feelings change after she saw Vandana grinning?
qa.a: At first she felt hurt, then relieved and amused once she realised it was friendly teasing.

qa.q: What helped Rajni read the teasing correctly?
qa.a: Noticing Vandana's grin and remembering that she teases people she likes.

qa.q: What would change if Vandana had said it with a frown and walked away?
qa.a: The same words might have felt mean, and Rajni could have taken it as an insult.

grounding: A girl reads her cousin's sarcastic joke about burnt toast as friendly teasing rather than meanness.

passage:
"Parveen, why did the maths book look so sad?"
"Why?"
"Because it had too many problems!"
Parveen rolled her eyes but smiled. "That's so old."
Bhavna grinned. "Okay, okay. What do you call a sleeping bull?"
"What?"
"A bulldozer!"
Parveen laughed. "Okay, that's good."
"And your drawing today? A real masterpiece. Museums will fight over it."
Parveen's smile dropped. "You think it's bad?"
"No! I'm joking. It was nice. The cat was cute."
"Oh." Parveen relaxed. "Then they can fight. I'm not selling."
"Exactly!"

qa.q: What do you call a sleeping bull, according to Bhavna?
qa.a: A bulldozer.

qa.q: What was Parveen feeling when her smile dropped?
qa.a: She felt hurt and unsure, thinking Bhavna was mocking her drawing.

qa.q: What helped clear up the misunderstanding?
qa.a: Bhavna quickly explained she was joking and said something kind about the cat.

qa.q: How might Bhavna feel when Parveen's smile dropped?
qa.a: Bhavna likely felt worried and sorry that her tease had landed wrong.

grounding: Two girls trade puns, and one briefly misreads a tease as meanness before understanding it.

passage:
The first time I understood a pun, I was nine.

Dilnaz asked me, "Why did the maths book look sad?"

I said, "I don't know. Because it's boring?"

"Because it had too many problems!"

I didn't get it for a whole minute. Then I did, and I laughed so loudly the teacher looked at us.

After that, I started collecting riddles in a notebook. I tried them on everyone at home.

I'm Preeti, and now I'm the one telling the bad jokes.

qa.q: What did Dilnaz say the maths book had?
qa.a: Dilnaz said it had too many problems.

qa.q: How did Preeti feel when the pun made sense?
qa.a: Preeti felt delighted and surprised, laughing so loudly the teacher looked.

qa.q: How could the family support Preeti's love of wordplay?
qa.a: They could listen to Preeti's riddles, share their own, and enjoy the jokes together.

qa.q: How might Dilnaz feel when Preeti finally laughed?
qa.a: Dilnaz likely felt pleased that the joke worked.

grounding: A child remembers first understanding a pun and enjoying wordplay.

passage:
Lohri party note.

At the class Lohri party, Baljeet tripped carrying peanuts and spilled them everywhere. Sabina said, "Wow, great job, Baljeet!" with a big smile.

A year ago, Baljeet might have cried. Today he looked at her, saw her grin, and said, "Thank you, I practise every day." Everyone laughed, including Sabina.

He understood it was teasing, not meanness. They picked up the peanuts together, still giggling, and Baljeet saved the last handful for Sabina. — class teacher

qa.q: What did Baljeet spill?
qa.a: He spilled the peanuts everywhere.

qa.q: How did Baljeet feel when Sabina teased him?
qa.a: Baljeet felt amused and relaxed, seeing it as friendly teasing.

qa.q: What did Baljeet do that showed understanding of humour?
qa.a: He read Sabina's grin and replied with a joke, instead of taking it as meanness.

qa.q: How might Sabina feel when Baljeet joked back?
qa.a: Sabina likely felt relieved and happy that he got the joke.

grounding: A teacher notes a boy understanding sarcasm as friendly teasing at a Lohri party.

passage:
Eid, Monday

Arnab Bhai came for sheer khurma. The first thing he said was, "Parveen, you're so tall now, can you see Lahore from there?"

Last year I would have felt bad. I'm the tallest in my class and people tease me.

But today I saw he was smiling and his eyes were kind. So I said, "Yes, and I can see your bald spot too."

He laughed so much he spilled his sheer khurma. Ammi laughed too.

I think teasing is okay when you both laugh.

Parveen

qa.q: What did Arnab Bhai ask Parveen?
qa.a: He asked, "Parveen, you're so tall now, can you see Lahore from there?"

qa.q: How did Parveen feel about the teasing this year?
qa.a: Parveen felt amused and confident, seeing Arnab Bhai's kind smile.

qa.q: How did Parveen tell the difference between teasing and meanness?
qa.a: Parveen noticed his smiling face and kind eyes, and that they both laughed.

qa.q: How might Arnab Bhai feel when Parveen joked back?
qa.a: Arnab Bhai was amused and delighted, laughing hard.

grounding: On Eid, a child understands a cousin's lighthearted teasing and responds with wit.

passage: At the Baisakhi mela in their village, Amandeep bought a paper windmill and ran round until it spun. His cousin Ira grinned. "Careful, Aman, you're so full of hot air you'll take off with it." Amandeep stopped. His ears went red. "You're calling me a show-off?" Ira laughed. "No, silly. Hot air. Windmill. Get it?" Amandeep looked at the spinning paper, then at Ira's face, all crinkles, not mean at all. He snorted. "Then you're so slow you'd need a tractor to turn yours." Ira clutched her stomach laughing, and they raced to the next stall.

qa.q: What did Amandeep buy at the Baisakhi mela?
qa.a: He bought a paper windmill.

qa.q: What did Amandeep's red ears suggest at first?
qa.a: They suggest he felt hurt and embarrassed, thinking Ira was calling him a show-off.

qa.q: How did Amandeep work out that the tease wasn't mean?
qa.a: He saw the joke's link to the windmill and noticed Ira's crinkled, friendly face, then answered with a joke of his own. 😄

qa.q: What would change if Ira hadn't explained the joke?
qa.a: Amandeep might have stayed hurt, and Ira might never have known the joke had stung.

grounding: Shows a child first mistaking a cousin's pun for an insult, then getting the joke and teasing back.
